INTRODUCTIONM
In this lesson, you will study the 8051 microcontroller in detail. You will learn about the internal structure of the 8051 including the registers, ALU, and the control sections.

It is important to realize that both microcontrollers and microprocessors work the same internally. Microcontrollers are used in applications such as automobile control systems, medical instrumentation and appliances, where the tasks and programming remain equipment specific. Microprocessors are used in more versatile applications such as home PCs....................................

You will learn about the input and output signals of the 8051 integrated circuit. These signals are used to control the external microcontroller system elements and to transfer data between the microcontroller and the rest of the system.

After completing this lesson, you will be able to describe the structure and features unique to the 8051. For more details on the advanced features of the 8051, or any microcontroller, refer to the manufacturer's data book on that product.

8051 MICROCONTROLLER CIRCUITRY
The 8051 is an 8-bit microcontroller. The internal registers are 8 and 16 bits wide. The external data bus of an 8051 microcontroller is also 8 bits wide.

DISCUSSION
The 8051 has a 16-bit address bus and thus the 8051 can address up to 2 or 65 Kbytes of memory.
The functional diagram of the 8051 is shown below.

You can see from the diagram that the sections of the 8051 microcontroller are connected by internal busses as you learned in earlier lessons. All communications within the microcontroller are performed by the combined effort of the data and control bus.
The address bus is primarily for addressing locations or devices external to the internal system. The data bus of the 8051 is 8-bits wide. This is why the 8051 is known as an 8 bit microcontroller.
Before we examine the sections of the 8051 in detail, let's look at a simple microcontroller instruction. The instruction is:

This instruction adds the 8 bit value in register R1 to the 8 bit value in the accumulator (register A) and places the result in the accumulator. This one operation causes many things to happen within the microcontroller.
A simplified list of the actions is given below............
a. Put the value of the Program Counter (PC) into the address buffer.
b. Drive the Address Latch Enable signal high and low.
c. The /Read signal goes low to indicate a read.
d. Read the 8-bit instruction from the data bus.
a. Move the instruction to the Instruction Register.
a. Move the 8-bit value of the accumulator register to the ALU.
b. Move the 8-bit value of the R1 register to the ALU.
From this example, you can see that registers, buffers, control sections, the ALU, and the internal data bus are all used to add these two numbers.
The operation of these elements must be controlled or coordinated by the control section of the microcontroller. The microcontroller performs many operations for each instruction that is executed.
In addition to the actions listed, the microcontroller must also check the status of the interrupt and reset signals while executing the instruction.
Now that you have an idea of what steps the microcontroller must perform for a basic instruction, let's look at the sections of the 8051 microcontroller in detail.
It is here that you will see a breakdown of each element in the 8051 block diagram and how they correspond to one another.
REGISTERS

The internal registers are where data and addresses are stored temporarily inside the microcontroller. The data in the registers can be accessed and changed much faster than data in external memory. Let's look at a brief summary of each register.
The accumulator (A register) is used for arithmetic, logic, load, and store operations. The accumulator is normally used with the B register for certain arithmetic operation.

The B register is used, along with the A register, for multiplication and division. When a number in A is multiplied with a number in B, a 16-bit result is formed and contained within A and B. In division, B will contain the remainder of the division.

The stack pointer (SP) is a special address register that always points to the current location in memory that is the top of the stack. A stack is a block of consecutive memory locations where data is stored like a stack of papers. You must take papers off the stack to see what is below them.
The Program Counter (PC) always points to the memory location of the next instruction to be executed. The registers always contains a 16-bit address.
The Program Status Word (PSW) register is an 8-bit register that uses each of the 8 bits to indicate certain conditions within the system.

P0, P1, P2, and P3 are used to control the ports of the 8051 microcontroller. The microcontroller can be programmed not to have address and data lines or control signals. With these registers the operation of the system can be changed.

We will look at the standard uses of these ports. Port 0 is used for the multiplexed address and data lines AD0 - AD7. Port 1 is used as a parallel communications port. Port 2 is used as the high 8 bits of the address bus. P3 is used for the control signals and a serial communications port.

R0 through R7 are general purpose registers which are used by many different instructions of the 8051 microcontroller. Each of these registers are 8 bits wide. In other microcontroller systems, these types of registers are referred to as data registers.

The DPH and DPL form the DPTR or Data Pointer Register. This register is used to access external memory. In other words, this register is effectively an address register as compared to other microprocessor systems.
When accessing external locations, it is the address in this register, DPTR, that will be used to retrieve data.

TH1, TL1, TH0, TL0, TMOD, and TCON registers are used to control and manipulate the internal timers built into the 8051 system. These timers are controlled through register settings and certain instructions. TH0 and TL0 along with TH1 and TL1 form two 16-bit registers known as T0 and T1. These are referred to as the timer registers.

The IP and IE registers are used for interrupt control. IP is the Interrupt Priority Register. This allows you to prioritize the interrupts being sent to the microcontroller. The IE register is the interrupt enable register. This register allows you to enable or disable interrupts in the system.

The PCON or Power Control Register is used to control a variety of different functions within the system. Some of these functions include serial port speed, general purpose flags, idle mode bit, and a power down bit.

SBUF and SCON are used by the built in serial port of the 8051 system. Data being transmitted or received can be obtained or sent to the SBUF register, otherwise known as the serial buffer register. The SCON or serial control register is used to program the operation of the serial port.

Also, not shown are internal buffers which are used to temporarily hold data or addresses that are exchanged within the address and data busses, and the instruction register. Remember, the instruction register holds instruction that is currently being executed.

Data is transferred between registers or between a register and another section of the microcontroller on the internal data bus. The control blocks control the flow of the data within the microcontroller.
Unlike many other microprocessor systems, the 8051 microcontroller has many special internal registers. The 8051 also contains internal RAM on most models.
The 8051 was designed to minimize circuitry in embedded control operations. This makes circuits used in devices like microwaves or televisions smaller, more reliable, and less expensive.

There are many different versions of the 51 family microcontroller. The version used on the Nida 8051 trainer is the 8031. The 8031 microcontroller differs from the 8051 in that it contains no ROM built into the microcontroller.
The Nida 8051 trainer uses a separate IC for EEPROM memory. This allows us to look at certain signals that would otherwise be hidden within the 8051 IC.
Further, many of the registers within the 8051 can be accessed at the bit level. There are many bit instructions that allow you to manipulate certain bits within the registers.
Bit level register access will not be covered in these lessons. For more information, refer to the 8051 data book.

The arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) of the 8051 microcontroller performs all the arithmetic and logic operations for the system. The ALU can add, subtract, increment, decrement, AND, OR, XOR, compare, rotate, and complement.
INSTRUCTION
Depending on the conditions of the results, certain flags will be set in the program status word register. These can indicate problems or conditions with the last generated result from the ALU.
If the values you add result in a number larger than 8-bits can show, a carry flag is generated. This indicates that the number actually has an additional bit in the 9th slot.
When using an 8-bit addition to add 16-bits, the second addition of the upper 8-bits has to include the addition of the carry if it occurred. Without this, the addition would be incorrect.
The graphic below is an example of an addition. The instruction decoder has told the ALU, via the control section, that the operation to perform is an addition.

After all the data has been moved into place the control register tells the ALU to execute the instruction. The result of the operation is placed in a location dictated by the instruction and the control section. The FLAGS of the program status word register are set or reset according to the result.
For a complete list of the arithmetic and logic operations that the 8051 is capable of performing, you should consult an 8051 microcontroller data book.
TIMING AND CONTROL
The timing and control block includes the circuitry for the internal clock and timer signals, the RESET signal, and for generating the external memory control signals.
REGISTERS
INTERRUPT CONTROLL
ADDRESS BUS
CONTROL BUS
In the next lesson, you will see how important the timing and control signals are for the proper transfer of information from external devices to the microcontroller, and vice versus.
If the timing is not correct, the device will begin conflicting with others and/or incorrect data will result.
INTERRUPT CONTROL
This block allows the microcontroller to stop whatever operation is being performed and service an external device such as a keyboard.
REGISTERS
INTERRUPT CONTROLL
ADDRESS BUS
CONTROL BUS
TIMING AND CONTROL
Without interrupts, the currently executing program would have to repeatedly check or poll each external device to see if the device was ready to transfer data between itself and the microcontroller.

For example, when you press a key on the keyboard of an IBM personal computer, an interrupt is generated and the computer stops executing the current program and stores the keystroke in a buffer. The computer then continues execution of the program.

The NIDA 8051 microcontroller card set does not use an interrupt for the keyboard. Instead the keyboard circuits are repeatedly polled to see if a key has been pressed. There are advantages and disadvantages to both methods.
When the microcontroller receives an interrupt, it stops executing the current program and executes another program to specifically deal with that interrupt.
Once the interrupt is processed, the microcontroller returns to the program it was executing when the interrupt occurred.

When an interrupt is called, the interrupt program must do several things so the original program register settings are correct when execution begins again. The list below indicates the minimum number of steps that must be performed by the interrupt program: Save the contents of any general purpose register that will be changed during the interrupt routine. 2. Service the cause of the interrupt. 3. Restore the contents of the registers. 4. Issue a RETURN instruction.
1. Save the contents of any general purpose register that will be changed during the interrupt routine.
3. Restore the contents of the registers.

These steps provide for correct interrupt recovery in the original program. If you modified registers and didn't restore them to their proper values, errors could exist in the main program data when execution resumes.
Now that we have looked at the different blocks of the 8051 microcontroller, let's look at the pin configuration (pin-out) for the microcontroller.

The pin configuration of the 8051 is shown below. Note that address pins 0 through 7 are also the data pins. Special circuitry will take the correct information from these pins at the proper time during operation. Having two signals on one line is known as multiplexing.

Pin 20 is the Ground or reference connection. Pins 32 - 39 are the A/D0 - A/D7 Multiplexed Address/Data Bus lines. In the beginning of a machine cycle this bus is the address bus, which becomes the data bus for the remainder of the cycle.
Pins 1 - 8 are P1.0 - P1.7 known as the Parallel Port. These are the pins of the built in parallel port. The parallel port has 8-bits and is controlled by certain internal registers.
Pins 21 - 28 are the A8 - A15 signals of the Address Bus. These are the high 8 bits of the address bus. There are no multiplexed data signals on these pins.
Pins 19 - 18 are the XTAL1 and XTAL2 signals which are used to connect an external crystal to the microcontroller. The 8051 has a built in timing circuit which requires an external crystal.
Pin 9 is the RESET Input. When this signal is set high, the microcontroller is reset and the instruction pointer is set to zero.
Pin 31 EA is the External Access signal. This pin indicates where to begin program execution. If high, the internal memory is used and when low then external memory is used.
Pin 29 PSEN is the Program Store Enable signal. This signal is used with external memory to indicate that an instruction is to be read.

Pins 12 and 13 are the INT1 and INT2 External Interrupt connections. The combination of signals on these two lines indicate one of three possible interrupts. A high on both lines indicates no interrupts to the microcontroller.

Pin 30 ALE is the Address Latch Enable signal. A latch is a bank of flip-flops used to store the last input value. The address latch stores the address from the multiplexed lines so it will be available for the rest of the cycle. The address latch enable tells the address latch it can take the information on the A/D pins.

Pin 10 and 11, TXD and RXD, are the Transmit and Receive signals. These two signals are used by the serial port of the 8051. These signals connect between the same two signals of another device to communicate. However, TXD of one is connected to RXD of another and vise versa.
Pins 14 and 15, T0 and T1, are the Timer External Inputs. These two pins provide an external input for the T0 and T1 internal timers.
Pin 16, WR, is the Write Control signal. A low level indicates the data on the data bus is to be written to the selected memory address or I/O location.
Pin 17, RD, is the Read Control signal. A low level indicates the selected memory or I/O device is to be read and that the data bus is available for data transfer.
Pin 40 is the Vcc or Power signal to the 8051 microcontroller. It is this signal that is used to apply +5 volts to the system.

As you learn more about the interface between the microcontroller and external circuitry, the purpose for these signals will become more apparent. In the experiment you will be able to look at any of these signals and compare them with other signals in the system.

EXPERIMENT
The PC130-405 card contains an 8051 microcontroller, address latches, serial buffers, serial port, EPROM, RAM, chip select decoding circuitry, and timing circuitry.

The rest of the components are resistors, capacitors, and a switch. There are also numerous test points for testing the signals in the system. The 34 pin connector is used to apply signals to the other devices of the system.
Since the keyboard is required for the basic operation of the 8051 microcontroller system, let's look at how the keyboard works.

The keyboard contains 24 keys. Each of the keys has its function(s) screened on the key surface. Some keys are used for more than one function. The keys that will be used in the experiment are described below.
0 - F These keys are used for entering hexadecimal numbers. Data and addresses are entered using these keys.

Edit This key is used to edit data in RAM. When you press this key, the LCD will show "EDIT ADD:_ " The system is now waiting for you to enter a segment and offset. An example would be "553:53". The segment is 0553 and the offset is 0053.
Run This key is used to run a program in RAM or ROM. When you press this key, the LCD will show "RUN ADD : ". The system is now waiting for you to enter a SEGMENT:OFFSET to the program.
Enter This key is used to indicate a current program, that you have finished entering information for a particular task.

Entering programs into memory of the 8051 uses the EDIT function of the 8051 Monitor Program. Once you have pressed EDIT, you will be cued to enter an address to edit. The typical address we will use is 8000.

On the screen is the current address and the current value stored in that location. There are three things you can do at any address. Type a new value and press enter, press the down arrow to move to the next address or use the up arrow to move to the previous address.

Every time you type a value and press enter, you will automatically move to the next address. If you press enter without entering data, zeros will be stored at that memory location.

Always remember to use the up and down arrows for movement through your code. When a program is shown to you, it will include an address, Opcodes, Mnemonics, and a description. Start at the first address given and enter each opcode consecutively until you are finished entering the program.
